summary: This informational document gives a service provider's perspective on Software-Defined Networking (SDN), trying to clarify what SDN covers. It discusses requirements, issues, and other considerations.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains what software-defined networking can mean for a service provider. It describes ways to automate service delivery and the practical limits that network operators need to plan for.

subtitle: A service-provider view of what software-defined networking covers and what it demands.

tldr.problem: Service providers combine many technologies and tools to deliver network services, while static procedures can be slow to respond to changing customer needs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC frames SDN as techniques for deterministic, dynamic, and scalable service delivery, grouped around discovery, service negotiation, resource allocation, and feedback.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC offers a service-provider perspective, not a protocol specification. It stresses that SDN must work within device limits and alongside existing networks.

today: RFC 7149 is an Informational document that presents a service-provider perspective on SDN. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Service Providers Consider SDN
sections.content:
Service providers combine routing, traffic quality, security, and management functions to deliver services such as IP virtual private networks. These services involve many protocols and tools.

The RFC says static service procedures and long planning cycles can be slow to respond to changing customer requirements. Uncoordinated management tools can also make operations more complex.
sections.plainLanguage: Service providers use many tools to deliver network services. When each tool works separately, changes can be slow and errors are harder to manage.

sections.title: A Working Definition of SDN
sections.content:
The RFC defines Software-Defined Networking as techniques that help design, deliver, and operate network services in a deterministic, dynamic, and scalable way. Here, deterministic service delivery means controlling the service chain so the delivered service matches what was negotiated with the customer.

The RFC groups these techniques into discovery of topology and device capabilities, service exposure and negotiation, service-driven resource allocation and policy enforcement, and feedback that checks service performance.
sections.plainLanguage: In this RFC, SDN means using software techniques to deliver a service as agreed. The system discovers what the network can do, agrees service settings, allocates resources, and checks the result.

sections.title: Limits and Deployment Choices
sections.content:
The RFC cautions that separating forwarding and control planes is not new: many routers already separated software route computation from hardware forwarding. A logically centralized controller for route computation is a different matter.

SDN features remain limited by device hardware and software. OpenFlow is one possible protocol for carrying configuration, but the RFC names alternatives and says there is no one-to-one relationship between OpenFlow and SDN. SDN-capable devices must coexist with legacy systems, so deployment can be gradual.
sections.plainLanguage: SDN does not remove the limits of network equipment. Operators can add SDN techniques in stages, and they can use different protocols to communicate with devices.

sections.title: Bootstrapping and Operating an SDN
sections.content:
A Policy Decision Point (PDP) makes policy decisions, while a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) applies them in network devices. The RFC says an SDN needs ways to discover participating devices and their capabilities, connect the PDP without forwarding loops, check connectivity, and detect and diagnose failures.

Automation can simplify service work, but it also creates complexity beneath the automated steps. The RFC identifies testing, management, performance, scalability, and coordination among multiple PDPs as issues requiring attention.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller needs an accurate picture of devices and network resources before it can make decisions. Operators also need ways to test those decisions and handle failures.

sections.title: Security and Risk Assessment
sections.content:
The RFC treats security as necessary for reliable interactions among network components. Service providers should assess software modules, including how they behave under stress, how vulnerabilities are found, and how upgrades are performed.

PDPs and PEPs, and communication between PDPs, need appropriate authorization and protection. The RFC also recommends assessing interoperability, legacy-system impacts, and effects on capital and operating costs.
sections.plainLanguage: Controllers and network devices exchange instructions that affect service. Operators need to protect these exchanges and assess the software and operational risks.
